parts.label: (a)

markscheme_points.text: (for a system in equilibrium,) sum of clockwise moments (about a point) equals sum of anticlockwise moments (about the same point)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what must be true for turning effects when a beam is perfectly balanced and not rotating - compare the total turning effect one way with the total turning effect the other way about the same point.
parts.proper_answer: For a body in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point is equal to the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what a moment means**
Imagine trying to turn a see-saw. A moment is force times perpendicular distance from the pivot, $moment = F \times d$. It tells you how strongly something tries to rotate clockwise or anticlockwise.

Step 2: **Apply the equilibrium idea**
If the system is balanced, the clockwise trying-to-turn must exactly cancel the anticlockwise trying-to-turn. So for equilibrium: $$\text{sum of clockwise moments} = \text{sum of anticlockwise moments}$$ about the same point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A rigid uniform beam rests on a pivot at its centre, as shown in Fig. 3.1.

{{figure:figure_3_1}}

Fig. 3.1 (not to scale)

A load of weight $2.6\text{ N}$ is suspended from the beam at distance $x$ from the pivot.

A wooden cylinder of weight $4.0\text{ N}$ is suspended from the beam at a distance of $0.40\text{ m}$ from the pivot on the opposite side of the pivot to the load. The cylinder rests in a container of water. The lower part of the cylinder is immersed in the water to depth $h$.

Initially, $h$ is equal to $0.10\text{ m}$ and $x$ is equal to $0.40\text{ m}$. The system is in equilibrium.
parts.text: Use the principle of moments to show that the upthrust $U$ exerted by the water on the cylinder is $1.4\text{ N}$.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the right-hand side first - the cylinder has weight 4.0 N downwards but the water pushes up with upthrust U, so what is the net downward pull on the beam at 0.40 m from the pivot?
Hint 2: Now balance the turning effects about the pivot with x = 0.40 m on both sides, and rearrange to solve for U.
parts.proper_answer: Net force on right is $(4.0 - U)$. Taking moments about pivot: $2.6 \times 0.40 = (4.0 - U) \times 0.40$, so $4.0 - U = 2.6$ giving $U = 1.4\text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the real pull on each side**
On the left, the pull is simply the load: $2.6\text{ N}$ at distance $x = 0.40\text{ m}$. On the right, gravity pulls down with $4.0\text{ N}$ but upthrust $U$ pushes up, so the beam only feels the difference: $$F_{right} = 4.0 - U$$ This is a common trap - do not use 4.0 N alone when the object is immersed.

Step 2: **Balance moments about the pivot**
Anticlockwise moment = clockwise moment: $$2.6 \times x = (4.0 - U) \times 0.40$$ With $x = 0.40\text{ m}$ the distances cancel: $$2.6 = 4.0 - U$$ So: $$U = 4.0 - 2.6 = 1.4\text{ N}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
The density of the water is $1.0 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$.

Calculate the area $A$ of the circular cross-section of the cylinder.

markscheme_points.text: U = ρgV and A = V / h or p = hρg and A = U / p or A = U / hρg

hints: Hint 1: Remember upthrust comes from the weight of water displaced by the immersed part - link U to the immersed volume V using density and g.
Hint 2: The immersed part is a short cylinder of height h and cross-sectional area A, so rewrite V in terms of A and h.
Hint 3: Rearrange to make A the subject and check all units are SI before substituting h = 0.10 m, U = 1.4 N and density $1.0 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$.
parts.proper_answer: $U = \rho g V = \rho g A h$, so $A = U/(\rho g h) = 1.4/(0.10 \times 1.0 \times 10^3 \times 9.81) = 1.4 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link upthrust to displaced volume**
Upthrust equals weight of displaced water: $$U = \rho g V$$ where $\rho = 1.0 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$ is water density and $V$ is immersed volume.

Step 2: **Express volume with area and depth**
The submerged section is a cylinder of area $A$ and height $h$: $$V = A h$$ So: $$U = \rho g A h$$

Step 3: **Rearrange and calculate**
Make $A$ the subject: $$A = \frac{U}{\rho g h}$$ Substitute $U = 1.4\text{ N}$, $h = 0.10\text{ m}$, $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$: $$A = \frac{1.4}{0.10 \times 1.0 \times 10^3 \times 9.81} = 1.4 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2$$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
More water is gradually added to the container in (b), so that depth $h$ in Fig. 3.1 gradually increases. The length $x$ is continuously adjusted so that the system remains in equilibrium.

On Fig. 3.2, sketch the variation of $x$ with $h$. Use the space below for any working.

{{figure:figure_3_2}}

Fig. 3.2
hints: Hint 1: Start from what you know - when h = 0.10 m, x = 0.40 m, so mark that starting point and think how U changes if h grows.
Hint 2: Combine $U = \rho g A h$ with the moments equation $2.6x = (4.0 - U) \times 0.40$ to see what type of mathematical relation x has with h.
Hint 3: Think about when x would have to become zero - this happens when the beam needs no left moment, so what must U equal then and what h gives that?
parts.proper_answer: Straight line starting at (0.10 m, 0.40 m) with negative gradient, ending on the h-axis at h approx 0.29 m where $U = 4.0\text{ N}$ and $x = 0$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See why x must fall as h rises**
More depth means more displaced water, so $U = \rho g A h$ increases. The net pull on the right, $4.0 - U$, gets smaller, so its clockwise moment shrinks. To stay balanced the anticlockwise moment $2.6 \times x$ must also shrink, so $x$ decreases.

Step 2: **Show the shape is a straight line**
Put the two ideas together: $$2.6x = (4.0 - \rho g A h) \times 0.40$$ Since $\rho$, $g$, $A$ are constants, $x$ is of the form $x = a - b h$. That is linear with negative gradient. Start the line at the known equilibrium point: $$(h = 0.10\text{ m}, x = 0.40\text{ m})$$

Step 3: **Find where the line hits zero**
$x = 0$ means no moment is needed on the left, so the right side must pull with zero net force: $$4.0 - U = 0$$ $$U = 4.0\text{ N}$$ Using $U = \rho g A h$: $$h_{0} = \frac{4.0}{\rho g A} = \frac{4.0}{1.0 \times 10^3 \times 9.81 \times 1.4 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 0.29\text{ m}$$ So draw a straight line from (0.10, 0.40) down to (0.29, 0) on the Fig. 3.2 axes.
